Shadow tomography

General framework of shadow tomography

Single-copy shadow tomography restores single copy of \rho, repeats randomized measurements, and try to use these measurement results to estimate MANY properties of \rho, which includes linear property \text{tr}(O_i\rho), non-linear properties \text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}), and even their products \prod_{i}\text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}). The procedure of shadow tomography firstly includes the sampling of classical shadow, as shown in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow]. Note that in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow], virtually means restore the classical description of circuit U and length-n bit string \mathbf b. As shown in Lemma [lemma:single_shadow_unbiased], to estimate many properties includes \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k), ones compute based only those sampled classical shadow.

Sample U \sim \mathcal{U} with certain unitary ensemble \mathcal{U}. Measure the state U\rho U^\dagger on the computational basis with result \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}}. Virtually computes the shadow matrix \hat \rho:= \mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U), where \mathcal{M} is the entanglement-breaking linear map \rho \to \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{U}} \sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \rho U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \cdot U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} U.

ImportantLemma

The estimator \hat{o}^{(k)} := \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) is an unbiased estimator for the expectation \text{tr}(O \rho^k), where \hat{\rho}_i is sampled according to the Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow].

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) &= \mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger} \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]\\ &= \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger}U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]=\text{tr}(O \rho^k). \end{align} ◻

While we do not care about the computational complexity in the most case, the computation of \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k) can be reconstructed as \bra{\mathbf b}(U\mathcal{M}^{-1, \dagger}(O)U^\dagger) \ket{\mathbf b}, thus might be processed efficiently if the randomized unitaries U is classical tractable and the target operator O can be decomposed into poly(n) numbers of simple operators.

The sampling complexity of any classical shadows scheme depends on both the choice of unitary distribution \mathcal{U} and the particular set of properties O of interest.

The inverse channel \mathcal{M}

The explicit form of channel \mathcal{M} rely on the choice of unitary ensembles. Results of \mathcal{M} are known for global and on site 2-design unitary ensembles, 2-design unitary ensemble, fermionic Gaussian unitary ensemble, manybody Gaussian unitary ensemble, and locally scrambled unitaries ensemble. In this subsection we summarized these results.

ImportantLemma

A k-site 2-design unitary ensembles \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n} separates n\cdot k numbers of qudits in to n parts, and independently implements k-qudit 2-design unitary, as defined in Definition [def:t_design], within each part. In other words, \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n}:=\{\bigotimes_{i =1}^n U_i| U_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)\}. This ensemble induces the channel \begin{align} \mathcal{M}(\rho) = (\mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)})^{\otimes n}(\rho), \text{with~} \mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)}(\cdot) = \frac{1}{2^k +1}(\cdot) + \frac{\text{tr}(\cdot)}{2^k + 1}{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}. \end{align} Specifically, the global 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case n = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k),and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) ={(d^k + 1)^{-1}} \rho + {d^k{(d^k + 1)^{-1}} \text{tr}\rho \cdot }({\mathbb{I}(d^k)}/{d^k}). The local 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case k = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d)^{\otimes n},and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) = {(d + 1)}^{-1} \rho + {d({d + 1})^{-1} \text{tr}\rho} \cdot ({\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d}).

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. For tensor product inputs \otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i, \rho_i \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^k)), the channel \mathcal{M} in this case became \begin{align} \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i) &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} (\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i) \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}} \cdot \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} \notag\\ &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \text{tr}_{\bar A} \left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right)\cdot (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\! \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(A)} \right)\notag\\ &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_i \in \mathbb{F}_d^k} \mathbb{E}_{\substack{\text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(A)} \right)\notag\\ &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_{i}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{k}} \Phi_2(\ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{\otimes 2})^{(\bar A A)} \right)\notag \\ &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n d^{k} \frac{\mathbb{I}^{(\bar A)}(d^k)\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^k)+ \mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}}{(d^k+1) \cdot d^k}\right).\label{eq:k_copy_shadow_channel} \end{align} Here in the second line, we use the fact that \ket{{r}_x {r}_z} =H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \ket{\Phi_{r_xr_z}}, with H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \in \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k). If we expand \rho on separable basis \rho = \bigotimes_{i =1}^n \rho_{i}, plug in Eq. [eq:k_copy_shadow_channel], and use the fact that \text{tr}_{\bar A}(\mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}\cdot \rho^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}) = \rho^{(A)}, we get the channel output \begin{align} \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i) &= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \text{tr}(\rho_i) \frac{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}{d^k + 1} + \frac{1}{d^k +1}\rho_i = \mathcal{D}^{\otimes n}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i). \end{align} By the linearity of \mathcal{M}, we conclude that its inverse \mathcal{D}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}^{-1}(\rho) = (d^k + 1)\rho - \text{tr}\rho \cdot \mathbb{I}(d^k) constitute an unbiased estimator of \rho \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^{nk})) through the transformation \begin{align} \hat \rho_{U,\mathbf b} =\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\text{U}^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} \text{U})=\bigotimes_{i =1}^n\left((d^k +1)\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} \text{U}_i - \mathbb{I}(d^k)\right). \end{align} ◻

This 2-design unitary ensemble includes the Clifford randomized measurement and the randomized Pauli basis measurement, as proposed in  [huang2020predicting?]. Consider the unitary ensemble \mathcal{E} that Following the previous research, we review the estimation variance in the case with (i)the Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?,mele2024introduction?], (ii)the local Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?], and (iii). the Matchgate ensemble.

Global shadow and shallow shadows

The first case is the Clifford shadow. It turns out that this ensemble is suitable for low-rank operators O whose trace norm \text{tr}(O^2) is small. This condition is satisfied for entangled pure-state projectors but not for Pauli observables.

ImportantLemma

In the case of {U} \sim \text{Cliff}(2^n) and \hat{o}:= \text{tr}(O\hat \rho), we have: \begin{align} \text{Var}(\hat o)= \frac{(2^n +1)}{(2^n+2)}\left[\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right] - \text{tr}^2(O_0\rho) \leq 3\text{tr}(O_0^2) \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. To calculate the variance of this estimator, we note that \text{Var}(\hat o):= \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}_0^2 - [\text{tr}(O_0\rho)]^2, where O_0 is the traceless version of O. Then we give the value of \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 as \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &= \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U \rho U^\dagger} \text{tr}^2\left[O\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U)\right] =\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U \rho U^\dagger} \text{tr}^2\left[\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U\right] \end{align} This average can also be reduced to the Weingarten calculus through: \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &= \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cl}(n)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U\sigma U^\dagger}\bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}^2\\ &=\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}_2}\sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \rho U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} \bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}\\ &= \text{tr}\left[(\rho \otimes \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)\otimes \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O))\cdot \sum_{\mathbf b} \Phi_{3}(\ket{\mathbf{bbb}}\!\bra{\mathbf{bbb}})\right], \end{align} where the last step use the fact that the Clifford group forms a 3-design. Cite the Lemma [lemma:state_trajectory] again gives \begin{align} &\Phi_3(\ket{\mathbf{bbb}}\!\bra{\mathbf{bbb}}) = \frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_3} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)},\\ \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &=\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\rho) \mathrm{tr}^2(\mathcal{M}^{-1}) + \mathrm{tr}(\rho) \mathrm{tr}((\mathcal{M}^{-1})^2) +2\mathrm{tr}(\rho \mathcal{M}^{-1}) \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{M}^{-1}) + 2\mathrm{tr}(\rho(\mathcal{M}^{-1})^2)}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)}. \end{align} Use the fact that O_0 is traceless, \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O_0)= (2^n +1)O_0, we give the final result \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &= \frac{(2^n +1)^2\left[\text{tr}(\rho)\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right]}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)},\\ \text{Var}(\hat o) &=\frac{(2^n +1)}{(2^n+2)}\left[\text{tr}(\rho)\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right] - \text{tr}^2(O_0\rho). \end{align} ◻

Local shadows

The 3-design local shadow.

The second case is the local Clifford shadow, which chooses uniform ensemble on {U} \sim \text{Cliff}_2^{\otimes n}. It turns out that this ensemble is suitable for operators O that only supports on constant sized qubits. This condition, in contrast with the Clifford shadow, is satisfied for Pauli observables but not for entangled pure-state projectors. Given an operator O = \sum_{P} \alpha_{P} P decomposed on the Pauli basis, we have \hat o (\{U,\mathbf{b}\}) = \mathrm{tr}\left(O\hat{\rho}_{U,\mathbf{b}} \right) = \bra{\mathbf b}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}({O}) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} since \mathcal{M}^{-1} = \mathcal{M}^{-1,\dagger}. Use the fact that \tilde {\mathcal{M}}= (\mathcal{D}_{1/3})^{\otimes k} and the identity \mathcal{D}_{1/3}^{-1}(P) = 3P - \text{tr}(P)\mathbb{I} =f(P) P := \begin{cases}3P& \text{if~} P = X,Y,Z \\ \mathbb{I} &\text{if~} P = \mathbb{I}\end{cases}, we extend this definition to n-qubit case through f(P,Q) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(P_i, Q_i), with f(P_i, Q_i) = \begin{cases}3 \delta_{P_i,Q_i}& \text{if~} P_i,Q_i \in \{X,Y,Z\} \\ 1 &\text{if else}\end{cases}. Noted that U\ket{\mathbf{b}} is an eigenvector of Pauli operator P_{U} with eigenvalue s(U,\mathbf{b}). We conclude that \hat o (\{U,\mathbf{b}\})= \sum_{P}\alpha_P f(P,P_{U})s(\mathbf{b}). Then the variance of the estimator \hat{o} can be calculated below.

ImportantLemma

Given a the k-local operator with Pauli decomposition O =\mathbb{I}_{n-k}\otimes \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}(k)} \alpha_{P} P, the unbiased estimator \hat{o} above has variance \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{U,\mathbf{b}}(\hat{o}^2) =\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q \right) \leq 4^k\|O\|_{\infty}^2. \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Similarly, we first noted that given an observable O = \tilde{O} \otimes \mathbb{I}_{n-k} that supports on k-qubits, we have \begin{align} \label{eq:ave_of_square_LCshadow} \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} =\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)^{\otimes k}}\sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \tilde{\rho} U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \bra{\mathbf b}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(\tilde{O}) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}^2, \end{align} where \tilde{\rho} is the reduced state of \rho that supports on k-qubits. After this, we expand the k-qubit non-identity part within \tilde{O} into the linear combination of Pauli operators as \tilde{O} = \sum_{P \in \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes k}} \alpha_{P} P as well as the reduced state \tilde{\rho} = \sum_{s} \beta_s \bigotimes_{i =1}^n\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i. It is thus sufficient to calculate Eq.[eq:ave_of_square_LCshadow] pointwise as \begin{align} \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_{i = 1}^n \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} \!\!\!\sum_{b_i \in \{0,1\}}\!\!\! \bra{b_i}U \tilde{\rho}_j^{(s)} U^\dagger \ket{b_i} \bra{b_i}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(P_i) U^\dagger\ket{b_i}\bra{b_i}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(Q_i) U^\dagger\ket{b_i}\\ &=\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i)f(Q_i)\sum_{b_i \in \{0,1\}} \left[(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i \otimes P_i \otimes Q_i)\cdot \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} U^{\otimes 3}\ket{b_i}\!\bra{b_i}^{\otimes 3}U^{\otimes 3,\dagger}\right]. \end{align}

Again from Lemma [lemma:state_trajectory], \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} U^{\otimes 3}\ket{b_i}\!\bra{b_i}^{\otimes 3}U^{\otimes 3,\dagger} = (4 \times 3 \times 2)^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_3} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d =2}, which gives \begin{align} \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} = (\frac{1}{12})^n\sum_{P,Q}\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\sum_s \beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i)f(Q_i)&\left[ \text{tr}(P_i)\text{tr}(Q_i)\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)+\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)\text{tr}(Q_i) + \text{tr}(P_i)\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)\right.\notag\\ & \left.+\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\text{tr}(P_iQ_i) + \text{tr}(P_i \tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)+\text{tr}(Q_i \tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)\right]\label{eq:mid_sqr_ave}. \end{align} Depending on three cases, we calculate the RHS after the \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_i signal as \begin{align} \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n[\cdots] = \begin{cases} \prod_{i = 1}^n1\cdot 1\cdot [4+2+2+2+1+1] &\text{if~} P_i=Q_i = \mathbb I,\\ \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n1 \cdot 3 \cdot[2 + 1 + 1]\cdot \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)]&\text{if~} P_i = \mathbb I\neq Q_i,\\ \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n3 \cdot 1 \cdot[2 + 1 + 1]\cdot \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)]&\text{if~} Q_i = \mathbb I\neq P_i,\\ \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n3 \cdot 3 \cdot[2 +1+1] \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\delta_{P_i,Q_i}&\text{if~} Q_i, P_i \neq \mathbb I. \end{cases} \end{align} Here in the last equality, we use the fact that \mathcal{C}(P_i) = \{P_i, \mathbb{I}\} and \begin{align} \forall Q_i, P_i \neq \mathbb I, \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i \{Q_i,P_i\}) = \begin{cases}0 &\text{if~} Q_i \notin \mathcal{C}(P_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}\\2\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_iP_i) &\text{if~} Q_i \in \mathcal{C}(P_i)\backslash \mathbb{I} \end{cases} = 2\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\delta_{P_i,Q_i}. \end{align} Plug this equation into Eq.[eq:mid_sqr_ave] gives us the final results \begin{align} \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \left\{\begin{aligned} &\sum_{P,Q}\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q \text{~if~} P_i=Q_i = \mathbb I,\\ &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i \mathbb{I} \cdot Q_i)\text{~if~} P_i = \mathbb I\neq Q_i,\\ &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i\cdot \mathbb{I})\text{~if~} Q_i = \mathbb I\neq P_i,\\ &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i3\delta_{P_i,Q_i}\text{~if~} Q_i,P_i \neq \mathbb I \end{aligned}\right.:= \sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s \alpha_P \alpha_Q\prod_i f(P_i,Q_i) \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_iQ_i)\\ &=\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q \left(\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i,Q_i)\right)P\cdot Q \right):=\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q \right) . \end{align} To show the upper bounds, we noted that (i). If P,Q can both be obtained from replacing certain parts of S \in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k} with idendity \mathbb I, which we denoted as P,Q\subset S, then f(P,Q) \neq 0, and (ii). If f(P,Q) \neq 0, we count the number of position at which P_i = Q_i = \mathbb{I} as {k-|P\cup Q|}. Then this implies there are 3^{k-|P\cup Q|} numbers of S \in \{X,Y,Z\}^k s.t. P,Q\subset S. Such a non-zero value f(P,Q) is decided by the length of the overlap parts between P,Q\subset S, which satisfied f(P,Q) =3^{|P| +|Q| -|P \cup Q|}. This gives \begin{align} \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q &= \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\sum_{P,Q \subset S} 3^{|P\cup Q| - k}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q) P\cdot Q \\ &=\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\sum_{P,Q \subset S} 3^{|P|+ |Q| - k} \alpha_P P \cdot \alpha_Q Q = 3^{-k}\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\!\!\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|} \alpha_P P \right)^2. \end{align} Then we can upper bound the variance based on the fact that \sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|} = (3+1)^{|S|} = 4^k, \begin{align} \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &\leq 3^{-k}\left\|\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\alpha_P P \right)^2\right\|_{\infty} \leq 3^{-k} \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\alpha_P \right)^2\\ &\leq 3^{-k} \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\right) \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P|}\alpha_P^2 \right) = 4^k \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P| - k}\alpha_P^2 \right). \end{align} Notice that \forall P \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{k}, \exists 3^{|P| - k} numbers of S \in \{X,Y,Z\} s.t. P \subset S (S that generated from replacing \mathbb{I} within P by \{I,X,Y\}). This means that \begin{align} \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P| - k}\alpha_P^2 \right) = 4^k\sum_{P \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \alpha_P^2 = 2^k \text{tr}(\tilde{O}^2) \leq 4^k \|\tilde{O}\|_{\infty}. \end{align} ◻

The Local shadow above can be reframed into biased one and introduce adaptive strategy.

ImportantLemma

Application of single-copy shadows

Estimates linear properties.

Then we discuss the power of classical shadow in estimating exponentially many linear properties \text{tr}(O_i\hat \rho), \forall i \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, as shown in Problem [prob:linear_shadow] and Lemma [lemma:linear_sing_shadow] below.

Given output state \rho and any collection of operators \mathcal{O}:=\{O_1,\cdots,O_M\} with \|O_i\|_{\infty} \leq 1, to get enough classical descriptions that estimates \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall O_x \in \mathcal{O} within \varepsilon additive error and 1 - \delta success probability.

ImportantLemma

To solve Problem [prob:linear_shadow], We can either (i).measure on the eigenbasis of O_1,\cdots ,O_M separately, each one for \varepsilon^{-2}\ln(M/\delta) times, or (ii).use global Clifford shadow tomography and generate N = 2^{\text{rank}(\mathcal{O})}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(M/\delta) numbers of classical shadows.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. ◻

Unfortunately, Lemma [lemma:linear_sing_shadow] implies the inefficiency of global Clifford classical shadow in estimating linear properties \mathcal{O}, if \text{tr}(O_i^2) is exponentially large. A practical example involves \mathcal{O}:=\{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}, which we called the Pauli shadow tomography and requires sampling complexity N \sim 4^n \cdot n for case(i) and N \sim 2^n\cdot n for case(ii). Both of them are exponentially hard. Interestedly, there exists simple local two-copy strategy that solve the Pauli shadow tomography, as described in Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] below. Combining the lower bound proof in section [sec:lb_shadow], this manifests a sharp transition of sampling complexity between the single copy strategy and the two-copy strategy for Pauli shadow tomography.

Consuming only \mathcal{O}(n) numbers of \rho, Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] collects enough classical Bell shadow that are able to estimate |\text{tr}(\rho P)|^2 within constant error for each Pauli operator. The power of Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] derived from the common unbiased estimator for \text{tr}(\rho \otimes \rho \cdot \sigma_{\mathbf r} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf r})

n-qubit density matrix \rho and a set of target Pauli operator \{\sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(1)}},\cdots,\sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(M)}}\}. Collect enough classical information such that \forall i, |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}})|^2 can be estimated within \varepsilon additive error and 1 - \delta success rate. Implements N \sim 4 \ln(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2 times Bell measurement and restore the result \mathbf{r}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{r}_N with \mathbf{r}_i \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}. To estimate |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{y}})|^2, take the xz decomposition of \mathbf y = (\mathbf{y}_x, \mathbf{y}_z) Calculate the average and return R =({1}/{N})\cdot\sum_{i = 1}^N(-1)^{[\mathbf r_i, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z}.

After that, we show

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof of Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const]. We first show the unbiasedness. Use the property of Bell sampling in Theorem [theo: Bell_prob], we conclude that for \rho = \sum_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{u}} \sigma_{\mathbf{u}}, \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r} \sim P(\mathbf r)}(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z} &= \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} \text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \rho^* \sigma_{\mathbf{r}})(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z}=\sum_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} c_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{v}}^*\text{tr}(\sigma_{\mathbf{u}} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} (-1)^{\mathbf{v}_x \cdot \mathbf{v}_y}\sigma_{\mathbf{v}} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}})(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z} \notag \\ &=\sum_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} c_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{v}}^*2^n\delta_{\mathbf u, \mathbf v}(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y + \mathbf v]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z +\mathbf{v}_x \cdot \mathbf{v}_y} = 4^n |c_{\mathbf{y}}|^2= |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf y})|^2. \end{align} ◻

Discussion above can be generalized to c-copy strategy for the d = c Weyl-Heisenberg shadow tomography, as defined below

Given a n-qudit state \rho, design a sampling method to estimate the value |\text{tr}(W_{\mathbf{a}}\rho)| with a constant additive error \varepsilon for all n-qudit Weyl-Heisenberg operator \{W_{\mathbf{a}}\}_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{n}}.

Unlike the qubit-Pauli operator, in this case \{W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d}\} are mutually commutant because W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d} W_{\mathbf{b}}^{\otimes d} =\omega^{d[\mathbf{b},\mathbf{a}]} (W_{\mathbf{b}}W_{\mathbf{a}})^{\otimes d} according to lemma [lemma:properties_WHop] and \omega^{d} = 1. We thus find the common eigenbasis for operators \{W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d}\}_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^n}. In the case with n = 1, it turns out that those eigenvectors can be specified by labels I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d - 1} and q \in \mathbb{F}_{d} as \ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum_{k = 0}^{d - 1} \omega^{kq} \ket{(0,I) + k \mathbf{1}}, with X^{\otimes d}\ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \omega^{-q} \ket{\phi_{I,q}} and Z^{\otimes d}\ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \omega^{|I|} \ket{\phi_{I,q}}.

ImportantLemma

Define a coarse-grained projector \Pi_{s_x, s_z} = \sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x} \ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} and its tensor product operator \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}_x, \mathbf{s}_z}:= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \Pi_{s_{x,i}, s_{z,i}}. Then we have: \begin{align} (X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}, \quad \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} =d^{-2n} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{-[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d}. \end{align} The average of operator X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z} can be estimated by post-processing the d-copy generalized Bell measurement result \mathbf{s}\sim \text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\rho^{\otimes d}\right) on d-copy state \rho^{\otimes d} as \left|\text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right) \rho\right)\right| = \left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}}~\omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}\right|^{1/d}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. We note the relation that \begin{align} &X^{\otimes d} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{-s_z}\sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x}\ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{-s_z} \Pi_{s_x,s_z},\\ &Z^{\otimes d} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{s_x}\sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x}\ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{s_x} \Pi_{s_x,s_z} \end{align} For a d-copies of n-qudit state \rho^{\otimes d}, we get a generalized relation by defining the tensor product operator \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}_x, \mathbf{s}_z}:= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \Pi_{s_{x,i}, s_{z,i}} with \mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}^{2n}_{d} and symplectic product in finite field \mathbb{F}_d^{2n} as [\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}] = \mathbf{s}_x \cdot \mathbf{r}_z - \mathbf{s}_z \cdot \mathbf{r}_x, which write (X^{\mathbf{r}_x})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{-\mathbf{r}_x\cdot \mathbf{s}_z} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} and (Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{\mathbf{r}_z \cdot \mathbf{s}_x} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}. Product those two terms and use the fact that \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\Pi_{\mathbf{s}'} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} \delta_{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'} gives \begin{align} (X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'} \omega^{-\mathbf{r}_x \cdot \mathbf{s}_z} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} \cdot \omega^{\mathbf{r}_z \cdot \mathbf{s}_x'} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}'} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}. \end{align} Use the identity \sum_{\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}']} = d^{2n} \delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}'}, we get the inverse transition \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} =d^{-2n} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{-[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d}. This then gives \left[\text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right) \rho\right)\right]^{d} = \text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right)^{\otimes d} \rho^{\otimes d}\right) = \sum_{\mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}\text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\rho^{\otimes d}\right) and proved the result. ◻

Non-linear property.

Then we discuss the power of classical shadow in estimating the non-linear property \text{tr}(O\rho^k). Notice that \text{tr}(O\rho^k) = \text{tr}(O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}\rho^{\otimes k}) with O' = O\otimes \mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes (k-1)}. To estimate the non-linear property \text{tr}(O\rho^k) for k>1, directly applied the Clifford shadow and the local Clifford shadow to operator O'\text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n} on a k-copies system gives exponentially large sampling complexity. According to the lower bound shown in Lemma [lemma:Clifford_shadow] and Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow]. This is because \begin{align} \mathrm{tr}(O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}\cdot O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}) = 2^{n(k-2)} \text{tr}^2(O) ,\quad 4^{\text{supp}(O'\cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n})} = 4^{k\cdot n} \label{eq:singlecp_shadow_nonlinear} \end{align} are both exponentially large in the qubit number n.

Lower bounds

In this section, we try to present the exponential sampling complexity upper bound for the single-copy shadow methods in estimating (i). A bunch of high-weight Pauli average O \in \{X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n},\text{tr}(O \rho) and (ii) A bunch of second-order value O \in \mathcal{O}, \text{tr}(O\rho^2).

Reduction of problems

Linear shadows

We first reduced the linear-shadow task in Problem [prob:linear_shadow] into a new version of discrimination problem.

ImportantLemma

Given a set of operators \{O_x\}_{x = 1}^M such that \text{tr}(O_x) = 0, \text{tr}(O_x^2) = 2^n, if an algorithm \mathcal{A} estimates \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta, then this algorithm can distinguish two cases with success rate 1 - \delta: (i). the maximum mixed state, (ii) one of the states within \{2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x)\}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. In the case (i), we have \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 0, \forall x because O_x is traceless by definition. This means that M^{-1}\mathrm{tr}(\sum_{x \in M}O_x \rho) = 0. While in the case (ii), we know \exists x \in \{1,\cdots,M\} s.t. \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 3\varepsilon. Based on these observations, we design the algorithms below: (a). \forall x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, use algorithm that solves problem [prob:linear_shadow], we get result r_x such that \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) - \varepsilon< r_x < \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) + \varepsilon. (b). If \forall x, r_x <2 \varepsilon, accept case (i), If \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon, accept case (ii). Note that \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \exists x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) > \varepsilon, this means case (i) is impossible. Similarly, \forall x, r_x < 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \forall x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) < 3\varepsilon, which means case (ii) is impossible. Then we prove the correctness of the reduction. ◻

The reduction presented in Lemma [lemma:red_shad2distin] required computing \mathrm{tr}(\rho O_x) for all x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, which is computationally hard if M \sim \text{exp}(n). To fill this gap, one can reframe the distinguishing problem into an adversarial scenario.

  • Alice (the adversary) first choose \mathbf{x}_0 \in \{1,\cdots,M\} according to arbitrary distribution \mathcal{D}.

  • Then Alice chooses to send N-copies of state \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0}:= 2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x) or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d to Bob.

  • Bob repeatedly receives \rho and measures with restricted POVMs.

  • After measurements ends, Alice tells Bob \mathbf{x}_0 and Bob decides whether Alice choose \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0} or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d through classical post-processing.

We say Bob wins this game if his decision is coincident to Alice’s choice. If there exists a shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} for \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta using N copies, then no matter how Alice changes the distribution \mathcal{D}, Bob can win the game with probability 1 - \delta by first run the shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} and then check the value of \mathrm{tr}(O_{\mathbf{x}_0} \rho).

Non-linear shadows.

For the non-linear Pauli shadow \mathrm{tr}(\rho^2P), we proved similar reduction by substitutes P into O_P := 2^{-1}(P \otimes \mathbb{I} +\mathbb{I}\otimes P)\cdot \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}, as shown below:

ImportantLemma

Suppose an algorithm get classical shadow for \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^{2})\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} with additive error \varepsilon and constant success rate 1- \delta using 2N copies, then with the same success rate, its result can be used to discriminate mixed state ensemble \mathcal{E}_1 = \{\left(\mathbb{I}_{2n} + 3\varepsilon (P\otimes \mathbb{I}) \cdot O_P\right)/2^{2n}\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} from the maximumly mixed state \mathbb{I}_{2n}/2^{2n}.

ImportantLemma

Suppose an algorithm get classical shadow for \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^{2})\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} with additive error \varepsilon and constant success rate 1- \delta, then with the same success rate, its result can be used to discriminate mixed state ensemble \mathcal{E}_1 = \{\left(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P\right)/d\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} from the ensemble \begin{align} \mathcal{E}_2 := \left\{\mathrm{Cl}^\dagger \left(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon Z}{2} \otimes \psi \right) \mathrm{Cl}\right\}_{\mathrm{Cl} \in \mathrm{Cliff}_{n}(\mathcal{O}), \psi \sim \mathrm{Haar}_{n-1}},\label{eq:nshd_red_ensem} \end{align} where \mathrm{Cl} \in \mathrm{Cliff}_{n}(\mathcal{O}) includes all possible Clifford gates that map Z \otimes \mathbb{I} to P \in \mathcal{O}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Supposed we design an algorithm that estimates \{\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^{2})\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} with \varepsilon-additive error and 1 - \delta correction rate. Then for mixed state \rho_0 = (\mathbb{I} + 3 \varepsilon P_0)/d in \mathcal{E} _1, estimation gives result \mathrm{tr}(P_0\rho^{2}) = 6d^{-1}\varepsilon and vanish for others. For state \rho = \mathrm{Cl}_0^\dagger \left(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon Z}{2} \otimes \psi \right) \mathrm{Cl}_0 in \mathcal{E}_2, we take P_0 \in \mathcal{O} such that \mathrm{Cl}_0 P_0 \mathrm{Cl}_0^\dagger = Z \otimes \mathbb{I}_{n-1}. The estimation of \mathrm{tr}(P_0\rho^{2}) then gives the result \begin{align} \mathrm{tr}(P_0\rho^{2}) = \mathrm{tr}\left(P_0\mathrm{Cl}_0^\dagger \cdot\left(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon Z}{2} \right)^2\otimes \psi \cdot \mathrm{Cl}_0\right) = \mathrm{tr}\left[\left(Z\cdot\frac{(1 + 9\varepsilon^2)\mathbb{I} + 6\varepsilon Z}{4} \right)\otimes (\mathbb{I}_{n-1} \cdot \psi) \right] = 3 \varepsilon. \end{align} Considering the \varepsilon additive error, we can then discriminate \mathcal{E}_1 and \mathcal{E}_2 by choosing \varepsilon_{\mathrm{th}} \in [(6d^{-1} + 1)\varepsilon, 2 \varepsilon] and checking whether there exists P_0 \in \mathcal{O} with \mathrm{tr}(P_0\rho^{2}) > \varepsilon_{\mathrm{th}}. ◻

In the discussion of strategy with replica restriction k < 4, we are free to replace \psi \sim \mathrm{Haar}_{n-1} to \psi \sim \mathrm{Cliff}_{n-1}. If we further choose \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n as all Pauli operators, the ensemble in Eq.[eq:nshd_red_ensem] can be further simplified as: \begin{align} \mathcal{E}_2^* := \left\{(1 + 3\varepsilon)/2\ket{0_L}\!\bra{0_L} + (1 - 3\varepsilon)/2\ket{1_L}\!\bra{1_L}\right\}_{\{\ket{0_L},\ket{1_L}\} \in C_{n}}, \end{align}

Multiple-copy Shadow tomography

Non-local strategy

We have proved the inefficiency of single-copy strategy while an efficient two-copy Bell strategy exists. In analogy, we try to break the lower bound in the last section by extending the single-copy shadow tomography method into the multi-copy case.

ImportantTheorem

Let \mathcal{P}_n be the n-qubit Pauli group. Let \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi} be the permutation operator on 2k replica of n-qubits (d = 2^n) and \pi =(\mathrm{odds})(\mathrm{even}) is 2-cycle permutation on odd labels (1,3,5,\cdots,2k-1) and even labels (2,4,\cdots,2k) respectively. For any P \in \mathcal{P}_n, define the operator: A_P =\mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] \cdot \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}. The family of observables \mathcal{A} = \{A_P\}_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} is a commuting family, i.e., [A_P, A_Q] = 0 for all P, Q \in \mathcal{P}_n. Furthermore, its expectation value on \rho^{\otimes 2k} is \mathrm{tr}(A_P \rho^{\otimes 2k}) = [\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)]^2. Therefore, a single projective measurement in the common eigenbasis of \mathcal{A} allows for the simultaneous estimation of |\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)| for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. We first prove the commutativity of the family \mathcal{A}. Let S_P = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] and abbreviate \pi = \mathbb{P}^d_{\pi}. The operators are A_P = S_P \pi and A_Q = S_Q \pi. First, \pi commutes with S_P, \forall P \in \mathcal{P} since S_P is symmetrized under repeat operation of \pi. Now, the commutator [A_P, A_Q] became: \begin{align} [A_P, A_Q] &= (S_P \pi) (S_Q \pi) - (S_Q \pi) (S_P \pi) \\ &= S_P (S_Q \pi) \pi - S_Q (S_P \pi) \pi \quad \text{(since $\pi$ commutes with $S_P$ and $S_Q$)} \\ &= [S_P, S_Q]\pi^2. \end{align} Finally, we show that [S_P, S_Q] = 0. This is because each term within S_P = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] and S_Q = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[Q^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] either have commutators of operators on disjoint subsystems or have two-replica terms with [P^{\otimes 2}, Q^{\otimes 2}] = [P \otimes P, Q \otimes Q] = 0. Thus we have [S_P, S_Q] = 0 for all Pauli operators P, Q . Thus, [S_P, S_Q] = \mathbf{0}, which implies [A_P, A_Q] = \mathbf{0}. We now calculate \begin{align} \mathrm{tr}(A_P \rho^{\otimes 2k}) &= \mathrm{tr}[\mathrm{sym}_{\pi}(P^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{\otimes 2k-2}) \pi \rho^{\otimes 2k}] = \mathrm{tr}[(P^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{\otimes 2k-2}) \pi \rho^{\otimes 2k}]\\ &=\mathrm{tr}[(P\rho \otimes \rho^{\otimes k-1}) \mathbb{P}^{d}_{(\mathrm{odds})} \otimes (P\rho \otimes \rho^{\otimes k-1}) \mathbb{P}^{d}_{(\mathrm{even})}]\\ &=[\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)]^2 \end{align} Thus, measuring the commuting family \{A_P\} simultaneously yields estimates for |\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)| for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n. ◻

ImportantLemma

If we can estimate |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|, \forall P \in \mathcal{O} \subset \mathcal{P}_n within constant additive error \varepsilon, then using a \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(|\mathcal{O}|)) times k-replica strategy with k \cdot n ancilla qubits, we can construct an estimator E_P such that |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^{k})| \leq 3\varepsilon.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Algorithmic proof of Lemma [lemma:signal_estim]. Denoting f_P = |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|. We then construct the quantum state \sigma such that \left||\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k)|- f_P\right| \leq \varepsilon. Such a state \sigma always exist and can be constructed if we knew an \varepsilon additive error estimator for \{f_P\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}}, but might cannot be found computationally efficient. Then we estimate \mathrm{tr}(\rho^k P)\cdot \mathrm{tr}(\sigma^k P) by measuring the commuting family \{A_P\}_{P\in \mathcal{O}} on state \rho^{\otimes k} \otimes \sigma^{\otimes k} for \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(|\mathcal{O}|)) times. This will give us an estimator g_P such that |g_P - \mathrm{tr}(\rho^k P)\cdot \mathrm{tr}(\sigma^k P)|\leq \varepsilon^2. Now we set E_P = 0 if f_P \leq \varepsilon and E_P = g_P/\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) if else. We thus noted that: \begin{align} \text{If~} f_P < 2\varepsilon, \quad |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| &= |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| \leq ||\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| - f_P| + |f_P| \leq 3\varepsilon \\ \text{If~} f_P \geq 2\varepsilon, \quad |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| &= |g_P/\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) -\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| = \frac{|g_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|}{|\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k)|}\\ &\leq \frac{|g_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|}{f_P - \varepsilon} \leq \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon - \varepsilon} \leq 3\varepsilon. \end{align} ◻

Examples.

In the case k = 2, the commutants we choose writes \{A_{\mathbf{r}} := {2}^{-1}{(\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbb{I}_n\mathbb{I}_n + \mathbb{I}_n\mathbb{I}_n\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma_{\mathbf{r}})} \mathrm{S}_{13}\mathrm{S}_{24}\}_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}}. Notice that \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}}} = (-1)^{[\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}]}\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}}}, the shared eigenbasis of \mathcal{A} have the form \ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} below with eigenvalues \lambda_{(s,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})} :=s \cdot 2^{-1}[(-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{a}]} + (-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{b}]}] and s = \pm 1. \begin{align} \ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}}&= \begin{cases} {2^{-1/2}}\left[{\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}} \otimes \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z} }+s \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z}} \otimes \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x\mathbf{a}_z}}}\right] & \text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}, \\ \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}}\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}}& \text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}. \end{cases} \end{align} After implementing the measurement \left\{\ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} \bra{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}}\right\}_{s \in \{+,-\}, \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} for T times and recording the results \{(s_t,\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{b}_t)\}_{t = 1}^{T}, the average of A_{\mathbf{r}} = \sum \lambda_{(\pm,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})} \ket{\Psi^{\pm}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} \bra{\Psi^{\pm}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} can then be estimated by calculating the estimator T^{-1}\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \lambda_{(s_t, \mathbf{a}_t,\mathbf{b}_t)}. To realize such a measurement, we refer to construction in  [liu2024auxiliary?] and noted that \begin{align} \ket{\Psi^{s}_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}}}&= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \cdot \begin{cases} 2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z} +s \ket{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z\mathbf{a}_x\mathbf{a}_z}}\right] &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\ \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b} \end{cases},\\ &= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\cdot \begin{cases} 2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} +s \ket{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z}} \right]\ket{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\ \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} \ket{\mathbf{0} \mathbf{0}}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b} \end{cases},\\ &= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\cdot \begin{cases} 2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}^{I}} +s \ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}}\right] \ket{\mathbf{a}^{E}}\ket{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\ \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} \ket{\mathbf{0} \mathbf{0}}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b} \end{cases}. \end{align} This disentangled the qubit on the third and the forth copy. Thus, we can locally implement the gate sequence \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{CNOT}_{34} and then measure the 3-rd and 4-th copies on the computational basis \ket{\mathbf{s}_{3}\mathbf{s}_4}. This gives the difference of vector \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} through \mathbf{s}_{3} = \mathbf{a}_x + \mathbf{b}_x,\mathbf{s}_{4} = \mathbf{a}_z + \mathbf{b}_z. This information then indicates a separtiton of the 1-st and 2-nd copies of qubits \{1,\cdots,2n\} = E \cup I, with E := \{i \in [2n]| a_i = b_i\} and I:= \{i \in [2n]| \bar{a}_i = b_i\} := \{i_1<i_1<\cdots<i_{|I|}\}. We then implement the computational basis measurement \ket{\mathbf{s}^{E}} on the qubits in set E and a GHZ state measurement s^{I} formulized by circuit: \begin{align} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}^{I}} + s\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}} \right] &= \begin{cases} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\bigotimes_{i \in I} X_i + Z_{i_1}\right) \ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~} s = -1,\\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\bigotimes_{i \in I} X_i + Z_{i_1}\right) \ket{{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~} s = +1, \end{cases}\\ &=\left(\prod_{i = i_1}^{i_{|I|-1}}\mathrm{CNOT}_{i,i+1}\right)^{\dagger} H_{i_1} \left(\prod_{i = i_1}^{i_{|I|-1}}\mathrm{CNOT}_{i,i+1}\right) \begin{cases}\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~}s = -1,\\\ket{{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~}s = 1.\end{cases} \end{align} Here we use the fact that since \mathbf{a}< \mathbf{b}, we have a_{i_1} = 0. This then gives the \mathbf{a} vector through \mathbf{a}^{E} = {\mathbf{s}^{E}} and s = +1, \mathbf{a}^{I} = {s}^{I} if a_{i_1} = 0, s = -1, \mathbf{a}^{I} = \bar{s}^{I} if a_{i_1} = 1.

The construction above is useful in generalization to general non-linear shadow  [liu2024auxiliary?]. To get a classical shadow of \hat{\rho^t}, analogically, we sample h(\mathbf b,V):=\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) with pseudo-probability \text{Pr}(V)\cdot\text{Pr}(\mathbf b|V): = \text{Pr}(V)\cdot\bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}. This gives the result \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{U}}\sum_{\mathbf b}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} = \rho^{t}. But \text{Pr}(\mathbf b|V): = \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} is not a valid probability distribution. Fortunately, it can be effectively realized based on the estimator of \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} in Lemma [lemma:gen_swap_est]. Note that the computational projective operator \{\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^{n}} is mutually commutant and the operator set \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b}, where Q_{\mathbf{b}}:=\text{sym}(\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}) = t^{-1} \sum_{i =1}^{t} \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}}_i fully distinguished the spectrum of \text{SWAP}_t^{\otimes n}. We use the common eigenvectors \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}} of the operator set \{\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\}\cup \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^n} and calculates \begin{align} \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} =f(\mathbf{x})\text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V) , \text{~where~}\left\{\begin{aligned} &f(\mathbf{x}):= \bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}, \\ &\text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x):=\bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}},\\ &\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V):=\bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}(V\rho V^\dagger)^{\otimes t}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}.\end{aligned}\right. \label{eq:tpower_shadow} \end{align} Here \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n\cdot t} labeled different eigenvectors. Then sampling h(\mathbf b,V) with pseudo-probability \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} then is equivalent to sample f(\mathbf{x})h(\mathbf b,V) with probability \text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V)\text{Pr}(V). If we can build an efficient quantum circuit \mathcal{R}\ket{\mathbf x} = \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}, this sampling can be realized. Based on this, we first give the form of common eigenvectors \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}} and then discuss the efficient implementation of \mathcal{R}. Because (\text{SWAP}_{t})^{t} = \mathbb{I}, \text{SWAP}_t must have eigenvalue e^{i2\pi/t}. This conclusion generalized to Lemma [lemma:eigvec_QSWAP] below.

ImportantLemma

Given \mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{z}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{z}_t) \in (\{0,1\}^{n})^t with set [\mathbf{z}]:= \{\mathbf z,\tau(\mathbf z),\cdots,\tau^{|[\mathbf z]|-1}(\mathbf z)\}, where the t-cyclic permutation \tau satisfied \tau\circ(\mathbf{z}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{z}_t) = (\mathbf{z}_{\tau(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{\tau(t)})=(\mathbf{z}_t,\mathbf{z}_1\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{t-1}), the operators \{\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\}\cup \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^n} have common eigenvectors labeled by [\mathbf{z}],k =0,\cdots, |[\mathbf{z}]|-1 as \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} \ket{\tau^{r}(\mathbf z)}, with eigenvalue \{e^{-2k\pi i/|[\mathbf{z}]|}\} \cup \{t^{-1}\cdot \# (\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}_i)\}.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. This can be proved by direct calculation. \begin{align} &\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n} \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} \ket{\tau^{r+1}(\mathbf z)} = e^{-2k\pi i/|[\mathbf{z}]|}\ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}}.\\ &Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\tau^{r}(\mathbf z)} = t^{-1}\cdot \# (\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}_i) \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}}. \end{align} ◻

Examples.

Take t = 2, the eigenvectors writes \{\ket{\mathbf{s}\mathbf{s}}\}_{\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n}} \cup \{\sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}), \sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}-\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1})\}_{\mathbf{s}_1\neq \mathbf{s}_2 \in \mathbb{F}_2^n}, which counts 2^n + 2^n(2^n - 1) numbers of linearly independent basis, thus being complete. This leads us to find circuit that transform the 2n-qubits computational basis into these bases. Specifically, \begin{align} \mathcal{R} \ket{\mathbf{s}_1 \mathbf{s}_2} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} &\ket{\mathbf{s}_1 \mathbf{s}_2} &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 = \mathbf{s}_2 \\ &\sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}) &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 < \mathbf{s}_2 \\ &\sqrt{2^{-1}}(-\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}) &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 > \mathbf{s}_2. \end{aligned} \right. \end{align} This pinned down the measurement cirucit by two steps: (i).Check whether \mathbf{s}_1 = \mathbf{s}_2 by transversal CNOT gates, (ii).On the different parts, with length l < n and most significant position p_{m}, implements \bar{H}:= \sqrt{2^{-1}} (X^{\otimes l} +Z_{p_m}) on those qubits. The step(ii) involved non-local operation within one of the copies. This is why we named it non-local multi-copy (NLMC) shadow.

Efficiency analysis.

As summarized in Lemma [lemma:var_nonlocal_nonlinear_shadow], the variance of NLMC shadow to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho^t) with unitary sampled from V \sim \mathcal{E} is upper bounded by the variance of single-copy shadow to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho) with the same unitary ensemble V. This means that if O is (i).low weight Pauli operators or (ii)low rank operators, NLMC shadow will have \text{poly}(n) sample complexity by taking \mathcal{E} = \text{Cliff}_{n}, \text{Cliff}(2)^{\otimes n} separately, which is exponentially faster compared to single copy shadow tomography in Eq.[eq:singlecp_shadow_nonlinear].

ImportantLemma

Given (\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V) sampled from distribution \text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | V)\text{Pr}(V), the random variable \hat{o}_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V) := \text{tr}\left(\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) O\right)\cdot f(\mathbf x) is an unbiased estimator for \text{tr}(O\rho^t). The variance of this estimator satisfied \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V} \hat{o}_t^2 \leq \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \text{Pr}(V)} \sum_{\mathbb{b}} \bra{\mathbf{b}}V\rho V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b} \text{tr}^2\left(O \mathcal{M}^{-1}\left(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V\right)\right). \end{align} Here the RHS related to the variance to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho) with unitary ensemble V \sim \text{Pr}(V).

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. To show the unbiasedness, according to Eq.[eq:tpower_shadow], we noted that \begin{align} \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{b}) \sim \text{Pr}(\mathbf{b}|\mathbf{x})\text{Pr}(\mathbf{x}|V)}f(\mathbf x) \cdot V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V = \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{E}}\bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} \cdot V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V = \mathcal{M}(\rho^t). \end{align} ◻

Local k-copy 3-design shadow.

Now we consider the case that we can put \rho^{\otimes k} in quantum memory and then implement randomized k-qubits Clifford gate U = {U_i}^{\otimes n} with U_i \in \mathbf{D}_{3}(2^k) the k-qubits gate and forms 3-design. After this, we measured each qubit in the computational basis.

ImportantLemma

In the case of local k-copy randomized measurements on \rho^{\otimes k}, let the observable O^{(k)} acting on n\cdot k qubits have decomposition O^{(k)} = \sum_{W} \alpha_{W} W, where W = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n W_i and W_i \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes k}. Denoting \mathcal{C}(W) as the set of k-qubit Pauli operator that commute with W and \delta_{e,S} = 1 iff e\in S, we define a function R:\mathcal{P}_k^{\otimes n} \to \mathbb{R} as \begin{align} \label{eq:R_expression} R(W,W') = \prod_{i = 1}^n r(W_i,W'_i), r(W_i,W'_i) := \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if~}W_i = \mathbb{I}_k \text{~or~}W'_i = \mathbb{I}_k ,\\ (2^k+1) \cdot \frac{2^{k-1}\delta_{W_i,W'_i} +\delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k } }{2^{k-1}+1} &\text{if~}W_i \neq \mathbb{I}_k \text{~and~} W'_i \neq \mathbb{I}_k . \end{cases} \end{align} we have \langle (\hat{o}^{(k)})^2 \rangle_{\rho} =\text{tr} \left(\rho^{\otimes k} \cdot \mathbf{V}(O^{(k)}) \right), where \mathbf{V}(O^{(k)}) := \sum_{W,W'}\alpha_W \alpha_{W'} R(W,W')W W'. Specifically, if we take a local operator O^{(k)} = \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \left(\sum_{W_i \in \mathcal{P}_k}\alpha_{W_i} W_i\right), we have \mathbf{V}(O^{(k)}) :=\bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{W_i,W_i'}\alpha_{W_i} \alpha_{W_i'} r(W_i,W_i')W_i W_i'.

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. By Lemma [lemma:onsite_2design], we conclude that its inverse is \mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)}^{-1}(\cdot) = (2^k + 1)(\cdot) - \text{tr}(\cdot) \mathbb{I}_k constitute an unbiased estimator of \rho^{\otimes k} through the transformation \hat{\rho}^{\otimes k} =\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf r}\!\bra{\mathbf r} U)=\bigotimes_{i =1}^n\left((2^k + 1)U_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} U_i - \mathbb{I}_k\right). The second moment is given by \langle (\hat{o}^{(2)})^2 \rangle_{\rho} =\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathbf{D}_3(2^k)^{\otimes n}}\sum_{\mathbf r}\bra{\mathbf r}U \rho^{\otimes k} U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{r}} \bra{\mathbf r}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O^{(k)}) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf r}^2. Similar to the proof in Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow], we decomposed the operator O^{(k)} on the Pauli product basis W_i \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes k} that supports on those k qubits located at site i. By denoting W = W_1\cdots W_n, we have O^{(k)} = \sum_{W} \alpha_{W} W. According to Lemma [lemma:onsite_2design], the inverse channel \mathcal{M}^{-1} acts locally as \mathcal{M}_i^{-1}(W_i) = g(W_i) W_i, where the scaling factor g(W_i) is determined by g(W_i) = \begin{cases} (2^k+1) & \text{if~} W_i \neq \mathbb{I}_k \\ 1 &\text{if~} W_i = \mathbb{I}_k \end{cases}. Use this decomposition and again supposed \rho^{\otimes k} = \sum_{s} \beta_s \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \rho_i^{(s)}, where \rho_i^{(s)} \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_k), the result involves averaging over the k-qubit 3-design U_i \sim \mathbf{D}_3(2^k) as: \begin{align} \langle (\hat{o}^{(k)})^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \sum_{W,W'}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}\sum_{s}\beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n g(W_i)g(W'_i)\sum_{\mathbf{r}_i \in \{0,1\}^k} \left[({\rho}^{(s)}_i \otimes W_i \otimes W'_i) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{U_i} U_i^{\otimes 3}\ket{\mathbf{r}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_i}^{\otimes 3}U_i^{\otimes 3,\dagger}\right] \\ &= \sum_{W,W'}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}\sum_s \beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n 2^k p \cdot g(W_i)g({W'}_i) \Bigl[ \text{tr}(W_i)\text{tr}(W'_i)\text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i) + \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i)\text{tr}(W'_i) \notag\\ & \qquad\qquad\qquad + \text{tr}(W_i)\text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W'_i)+\text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i)\text{tr}(W_iW'_i) + \text{tr}(W_i {\rho}^{(s)}_i W'_i) + \text{tr}(W'_i {\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i) \Bigr]. \label{eq:mid_sqr_ave_2copy} \end{align}

Here we use the fact that the term \ket{E} :=U_i\ket{\mathbf{r}_i} is average over the 3-design states, yielding terms based on the formula \mathbb{E} [E^{\otimes 3}] ={d^{-1}(d+1)^{-1}(d+2)^{-1}} \sum_{\pi \in S_3} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{(d)} according to Lemma [lemma:state_trajectory]. With d=2^k, the prefactor per site is p = 1/(2^k \cdot (2^k+1) \cdot (2^k+2)). We evaluate the expression by considering terms for each site i, analogous to the single-copy proof of Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow]. Depending on three cases, we calculate: \begin{align*} \langle (\hat{o}^{(2)})^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \sum_{W,W'}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}\sum_{s}\beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n 2^k p \cdot \begin{cases} 1\cdot 1\cdot [2^{2k}+3\cdot 2^k+2]\text{tr}{\rho}^{(s)}_i &\text{if~} W_i=W_i' = \mathbb I_k,\\ 1 \cdot (2^k+1) \cdot[2^k + 2]\cdot \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W'_i)&\text{if~} W_i = \mathbb I_k \neq W'_i,\\ (2^k+1) \cdot 1 \cdot[2^k + 2]\cdot \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i)&\text{if~} W'_i = \mathbb I_k \neq W_i,\\ (2^k+1)^2 \cdot[2^k\delta_{W_i, W'_i}\text{tr}{\rho}^{(s)}_i + \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i\{W_i,W_i'\})]&\text{if~} W_i, W'_i \neq \mathbb I_k. \end{cases}\\ % &=\sum_{W,W'}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}\sum_{s}\beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n \begin{cases} % \text{tr}{\rho}^{(s)}_i &\text{if~} W_i=W_i' = \mathbb I_k,\\ % \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W'_i)&\text{if~} W_i = \mathbb I_k\neq W'_i,\\ % \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i)&\text{if~} W'_i = \mathbb I_k\neq W_i,\\ % \frac{2^k+1}{2^k+2} \cdot\text{tr}\left[(2^k\delta_{W_i, W'_i}\mathbb{I}_k +2\delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k} W_iW_i'){\rho}^{(s)}_i\right]&\text{if~} W_i, W'_i \neq \mathbb I_k. % \end{cases}\\ &= \sum_{W,W'}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}\cdot \sum_{s}\beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n \begin{cases} \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_iW'_i) &\text{if~} W_i=W_i' = \mathbb I_k,\\ \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i W'_i)&\text{if~} W_i = \mathbb I_k\neq W'_i,\\ \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i W_i W'_i)&\text{if~} W'_i = \mathbb I_k\neq W_i,\\ \frac{2^k+1}{2^k+2} \cdot\text{tr}\left[{\rho}^{(s)}_i(2^k\delta_{W_i, W'_i}+2\delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k})W_iW_i'\right]&\text{if~} W_i, W'_i \neq \mathbb I_k. \end{cases}\\ &=\text{tr}\left( \rho^{\otimes k}\cdot \sum_{W,W' \in \mathcal{P}_k^{\otimes n}} \alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'} R(W,W') W W'\right). \end{align*} To prove the second equality, we first defined \mathcal{C}(W) as the set of k-qubit Pauli operator that commute with W and \delta_{e,S} = 1 iff e\in S, otherwise \delta(e,S) = 0. Then we use the fact that \begin{align} \forall W_i, W'_i \neq \mathbb I_k, \text{tr}({\rho}^{(s)}_i\{W_i,W_i'\}) = \begin{cases}0 \!\!\!&\text{if~} W'_i \notin \mathcal{C}(W_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k\\2\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i W_iW'_i) \!\!\!&\text{if~} W_i \in \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k \end{cases} = 2\delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k} \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i W_iW'_i), \end{align} In the last equality, we use the definition \begin{align} R(W,W') = \prod_{i = 1}^n r(W_i,W'_i), r(W_i,W'_i) := \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if~}W_i = \mathbb{I}_k \text{~or~}W'_i = \mathbb{I}_k ,\\ (2^k+1) \cdot \frac{2^{k-1}\delta_{W_i,W'_i} +\delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}_k } }{2^{k-1}+1} &\text{if~}W_i \neq \mathbb{I}_k \text{~and~} W'_i \neq \mathbb{I}_k . \end{cases} \end{align} ◻

The inherient difference between the single-copy local Clifford strategy contained in the term \delta_{W_i, \mathcal{C}(W'_i)}. In the single-copy case, the center of P_i \in \{X,Y,Z\} satisfied \mathcal{C}(P_i) = \{P_i, \mathbb{I}\}. However, for example, for the two-qubit Pauli operators, more terms involved. We denote the n-qubit Pauli operators as \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \sigma_{{r}_{x,i},{r}_{z,i}} \in \mathcal{P}_n with \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{r}_x = ({r}_{x,1},\cdots,{r}_{x,n}),\mathbf{r}_z = ({r}_{z,1},\cdots,{r}_{z,n})) \in (\mathbb{F}_2^n)^2 and \{\sigma_{00},\sigma_{01},\sigma_{10},\sigma_{11}\} = \{\mathbb{I}, Z,X,Y = iXZ\}. We denote a \oplus b = a + b \mathrm{~mod~}2 = a + b - 2a\cdot b and \mathbf{a} \odot \mathbf{b} = (a_1\cdot b_1,\cdots,a_n\cdot b_n) with a,b \in \{0,1\}. In the following, we follow the Pauli multiplication rule as proved below \begin{align} \sigma_{\mathbf{s}}\sigma_{\mathbf{s}'} &= \bigotimes_{j = 1}^n i^{s_{x,j} s_{z,j}} X^{s_{x,j}}Z^{s_{z,j}} \cdot i^{s'_{x,j} s'_{z,j}} X^{s'_{x,j}}Z^{s'_{z,j}} = \bigotimes_{j = 1}^n X^{s_{x,j}+s_{x,j}'}Z^{s_{z,j}+s_{z,j}'} (-1)^{s_{z,j}\cdot s_{x,j}'} \cdot i^{s_{x,j}s_{z,j}+s_{x,j}'s_{z,j}'} \notag \\ &= \sigma_{\mathbf{s}\oplus \mathbf{s}'} (-i)^{(\mathbf{s}_x+ \mathbf{s}_x'-2\mathbf{s}_x\odot\mathbf{s}_x')(\mathbf{s}_z+\mathbf{s}_z' - 2\mathbf{s}_z\odot\mathbf{s}_z')} i^{\mathbf{s}_x\mathbf{s}_z + \mathbf{s}_x'\mathbf{s}_z'}(i)^{2\mathbf{s}_z\mathbf{s}_x'} \\ &=i^{\mathbf{s}_x'\mathbf{s}_z - \mathbf{s}_z'\mathbf{s}_x} (-1)^{(\mathbf{s}_x + \mathbf{s}_x') \cdot (\mathbf{s}_z \odot \mathbf{s}_z') + (\mathbf{s}_z + \mathbf{s}_z') \cdot (\mathbf{s}_x \odot \mathbf{s}_x')}\sigma_{\mathbf{s}+ \mathbf{s}'} := i^{\mathbf{s}' J \mathbf{s}} (-1)^{d(\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}')}\sigma_{\mathbf{s}+ \mathbf{s}'} . \end{align} Defined [\mathbf{s}', \mathbf{s}]:= \mathbf{s}_x'\cdot \mathbf{s}_z - \mathbf{s}_z'\cdot \mathbf{s}_x \text{~mod~} 2 as the binary symplectic product. Use this rule, we calculate \sigma_{\mathbf{s}}\cdot \sigma_{\mathbf{s}'}=i^{2\mathbf{s}_x'\cdot \mathbf{s}_z - 2\mathbf{s}_z'\cdot \mathbf{s}_x } (\sigma_{\mathbf{s}'} \cdot \sigma_{\mathbf{s}}) \Rightarrow [\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'] = 0, and show that \mathcal{C}(\sigma_{\mathbf{u}} )\backslash \mathbb{I}_k= \{\sigma_{\mathbf{v}}|\mathbf{v}\in \mathbb{F}_2^k,\mathbf{v}\neq \mathbf{0},[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}] = 0\}. This means that \delta_{\sigma_{\mathbf{s},\mathcal{C}(\sigma_{\mathbf{s}'} )\backslash \mathbb{I}_k}} = \delta_{\mathbf{s}, \{\mathbf{v}\in \mathbb{F}_2^k|\mathbf{v}\neq \mathbf{0},[\mathbf{v},\mathbf{s}'] = 0\}} = {\left(1 + (-1)^{[\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}']}\right)}/{2} and \begin{align} \label{eq:lc_Pauli_rescale} &r({\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{s}'}):=r(\sigma_{\mathbf{s}},\sigma_{\mathbf{s}'}) := \begin{cases} 1 &\text{if~}\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{0}\text{~or~}\mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{0} ,\\ \frac{2^k+1}{2^{k}+2} \cdot \left[2^{k}\delta_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{s}'} +1+ (-1)^{[\mathbf{s}',\mathbf{s}]}\right] &\text{if~}\mathbf{s} \neq \mathbf{0}\text{~and~}\mathbf{s}' \neq \mathbf{0} . \end{cases} \end{align}

A generalization of the variance operator \mathbf{V}(O^{(k)}) is to applied it to two operators O_\alpha,O_\beta, as defined below:

NoteDefinition

Given two operators with decomposition O_\alpha = \sum_{W} \alpha_{W} W, O_\beta = \sum_{W} \beta_{W} W with W \in \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes k}, the we defined the covariance operator as \begin{align} \mathbf{V}(O_\alpha,O_\beta) = \sum_{W,W'} \alpha_{W} \beta_{W'} R(W,W') WW', \end{align} where R(W,W') is defined in Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow_kcopy] before.

The covariance operator is important due to the Lemma below

ImportantLemma

Given an k-copy operator O = \lambda_{\alpha} O_{\alpha} + \lambda_{\beta} O_{\beta}, we have \begin{align} \mathbf{V}(O,O) = \lambda_{\alpha}^2 \mathbf{V}(O_{\alpha},O_{\alpha}) + 2 \lambda_{\alpha} \lambda_{\beta} \mathbf{V}(O_{\alpha},O_{\beta}) + \lambda_{\beta}^2 \mathbf{V}(O_{\beta},O_{\beta}). \end{align}

NoteProof (Click to expand)

Proof. Supposed the decomposition O_\alpha = \sum_{W} \alpha_{W} W, O_\beta = \sum_{W} \beta_{W} W, we noted that \begin{align} \mathbf{V}(O,O) &= \sum_{W,W'} (\lambda_{\alpha}\alpha_{W} + \lambda_{\beta} \beta_{W})(\lambda_{\alpha}\alpha_{W'} + \lambda_{\beta} \beta_{W'}) R(W,W') WW',\\ &= \sum_{W,W'} \lambda^2_{\alpha}\alpha_{W}\alpha_{W'}R(W,W') WW' +\sum_{W,W'} \lambda_{\alpha}\lambda_{\beta} \alpha_{W}\beta_{W'}R(W,W') WW' \notag\\ & +\sum_{W,W'} \lambda_{\beta} \lambda_{\alpha}\beta_{W}\alpha_{W'}R(W,W') WW' + \sum_{W,W'} \lambda^2_{\beta}\beta_{W}\beta_{W'}R(W,W') WW'\\ &=\lambda_{\alpha}^2 \mathbf{V}(O_{\alpha},O_{\alpha}) + 2 \lambda_{\alpha} \lambda_{\beta} \mathbf{V}(O_{\alpha},O_{\beta}) + \lambda_{\beta}^2 \mathbf{V}(O_{\beta},O_{\beta}). \end{align} Here at the last line, we use the definition [def:cov_oper] and the fact that R(W,W') = R(W',W). ◻

Application to \text{tr}(O \rho^k).

A critical application of this local multi-copy shadow is to use it to estimate the non-linear term \text{tr}(O \rho^k) for arbitrary operator O \in \text{Herm}(\mathcal{H}_n). In the case of k =2, \text{tr}((O \otimes \mathbb{I}_n) \text{SWAP}^{\otimes n}\cdot (\rho \otimes \rho)) is an unbiased estimator for \text{tr}(O \rho^2). If we decomposed the operator O on the Pauli basis, it turns out (O \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)\text{SWAP}^{\otimes n} = \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} (\sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \otimes \mathbb{I}_n)\text{SWAP}^{\otimes n}:= \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} O_{\mathbf{r}} Here below we use Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow_kcopy] to evaluate the covariance operator of O_{\mathbf{r}} explicitly.

ImportantLemma

If we take O_{\mathbf{r}}= (\sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \otimes \mathbb{I}_n) \cdot \text{SWAP}^{\otimes n} for Pauli operator \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} and denote \text{wt}(\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}) as the weight of this Pauli operator, then we have \begin{align} \mathbf{V}(O_{\mathbf{r}}, O_{\mathbf{r}'}) = (-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}']} \bigotimes_{j=1}^n \left( % \left\{ \begin{aligned} &({5}/{3})\cdot \sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j}\otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}'_j}~ \text{if~} \mathbf{r}_j, \mathbf{r}_j' \neq \mathbf{0}\\ &({1}/{2})\cdot \mathbb{I} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j} \text{~if~} \mathbf{r}_j' = \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{r}_j\neq \mathbf{0}\\ &({1}/{2})\cdot \mathbb{I} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}'_j} \text{~if~} \mathbf{r}_j' \neq \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{r}_j = \mathbf{0}\\ &(11/3)\cdot \mathbb{I}_2 \text{~if~} \mathbf{r}_j = \mathbf{r}_j' = 0 \end{aligned} % \right. \right) \end{align} Specifically, \mathbf{V}(O_{\mathbf{r}},O_{\mathbf{r}}) = \left({11}/{3}\right)^{n}\cdot \left({5}/{11}\right)^{\text{wt}(\sigma_{\mathbf{r}})} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}}.

v({\mathbf{r}}, {\mathbf{r}'}) &= \left(\frac{1}{2} \Pi_{\mathrm{sym}} + \frac{7}{6} \Pi_{\mathrm{asym}}\right)(\mathbb{I} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}'}) + \left\{\begin{aligned} &\frac{5}{6}\left(\sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j}\otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}'_j} +\sigma_{\mathbf{r}'_j}\otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j} \right)&\text{~if~} \mathbf{r}_j, \mathbf{r}_j' \neq \hspace{5em}\text{~if~} \mathbf{r}_j=\mathbf{r}_j'= \mathbf{0}, \\ &\left(\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{I} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j}+ \frac{5}{6}\sigma_{\mathbf{r}_j}\otimes\mathbb{I}\right) \text{~if~}
